texts.187g-S10v2a:
From One Community to a Movement

Experiment Before You Divorce

Experimenting with a different rule doesn't have to mean everybody goes out and buys new land right away. Try it inside the parent group first, then as a semi-autonomous project, and then, if it needs more independence, as a seed group nearby that still shares some tools, childcare, business or friendships. Splitting off completely should be just one step along that gradient, and nobody should have to do it just to be allowed to experiment.

Some experiments (like a different land system, or a different population size, or any number of rules that work together) can't be tried in a way that's cheap. They may look bad when they're starved of the assets they actually need. "We tried it in one room for three months" isn't always a fair test.

Federation Without Building Another State

If these communities are supposed to spread, somebody eventually has to solve the boring problem of how they stay connected without turning into a super-commune (that's essentially just another state, with a nicer logo). I'd like them to connect, help each other and move people and knowledge around, but also to stay distinct enough that they can learn from one another.

At a federation level, that outward purpose gets concrete. I see the need to spread healing practices, train people and seed new projects. It's also important to keep any one comfortable enclave from forgetting that it isn't the whole movement.

The Federation of Egalitarian Communities says it's rebuilding, and that's a good warning. It takes work to run a federation. Delegates. Records. Compliance. Coordinating resources. Holding meetings. Succession. Whatever dispute function it actually takes on. These things all take up labor and material capacity before any local crisis has eaten into them. If the legal or economic environment requires it, the federation also needs to have a budget of outside money. It might also be good to know that the work of federation doesn't have to be done by a single entity. Two communities might want to be closely linked as friends, and that doesn't stop both of them from also being part of a general federation. There can also be local clusters, or single-function institutions like the FEC's PEACH health pool, which isn't currently governed by the FEC delegates.

On a related point, cooperation also shouldn't quietly turn into merging. The FEC has full members and communities working towards becoming full members, and it also has Friends who may simply stay friends. People need the same practical freedom of movement between communities. Somebody can be free to move in theory, but if their housing, status, health coverage, records, labor accounting, travel costs, taxes and transition disputes all fall through the cracks, that freedom's just decorative. A thin interface can often do it, one that says who's responsible for what while somebody crosses between them, without every community's internal systems having to match.

Even if nobody uses money internally, communities still need an honest way to keep track of exchanges and obligations. A gift of food, pooled medicine, a vehicle or a tool on loan, trades of labor, emergency housing, a shared building project, a visit that's mainly for training or relationship building: they're all different events, and some of them create future obligations while others don't. The federation can keep track of these for each purpose, without having to put a value on them or require every exchange to be "even". If cash is used for transactions with the outside world, the same goes for grants and loans. Guarantees and shared enterprise commitments should be tracked separately too. Solidarity doesn't make every community liable for whatever the others owe, and it doesn't give anyone an unlimited claim on another community's labor and stores, or its land and tools.

And when two principles collide and you make a rule out of it, store not only the resulting rule but also the original hard case: what happened, which principles were involved, what the first judgments were, what was finally decided and why, whether anyone dissented, what the consequences were, and which version of the rule it was decided under. When the rule changes, re-run the case. Otherwise each generation gets to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.
